reader.decision_reason: The message shows the delete closes the gap, meets SR-12's 15-minute limit through the existing `ACCESS_TTL`, and costs one `DELETE` per password change with no added read in the middleware. The immediate-logout alternative costs a Redis read on every request and breaks the stateless design, so it is not justified unless the requirement changes.

reconstruction.problem: `change_password` in `api/auth/password.py` updates the password hash but never revokes the user's `refresh_tokens` rows. `refresh_session` does not check the password or when it changed. A stolen device keeps renewing its refresh token with a fresh 30-day expiry, so the exposure is indefinite, not just 30 days.
reconstruction.what_breaks: After a password change, other devices stay logged in. A thief with a stolen device can call `POST /auth/refresh` after the access token expires and keep renewing the session. SR-12 is violated.
reconstruction.fix: In `change_password`, run `DELETE FROM refresh_tokens WHERE user_id = %s` after the `UPDATE users` and before `issue_tokens`, ideally all in one transaction. Delete all of the user's rows, not all except the current device, because `device_name` is not a safe identifier. The middleware is unchanged. The thief is logged out within 15 minutes, when the access token expires and `refresh_session` finds no row.
reconstruction.cost: One `DELETE` per password change. The laptop gets a new refresh token. Logout takes up to 15 minutes, not immediately. A `refresh_session` call already in flight on the phone can insert a fresh row after the `DELETE`; a transaction narrows that window but does not close it. Whether `api.db` supports transactions is not checked.

reader.closing_answer: Yes, implement the delete in `change_password`, inside a transaction if `api.db` supports one. Check `api.db` first. If it has no transaction support, do the delete anyway and say so.
